title: Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy versus Open Surgery for Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational cohort studies
keywords: Magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT)
condition_or_topic: Drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) and surgical outcomes after temporal lobe resection (TLR) versus magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT).
clinical_background: Epilepsy affects up to 0.6% of the global population. Temporal lobe epilepsy can impair cognition and quality of life, while drug-resistant mTLE can cause frequent seizures despite optimal antiseizure medication. TLR is established as more effective than medical management for seizure control in drug-resistant mTLE, and MRgLITT offers a minimally invasive alternative. Direct comparisons of these procedures are scarce. Earlier analyses have often used shorter seizure follow-up periods, and assessing surgical outcomes also requires distinguishing unexpected complications from anticipated adverse effects and measuring visual field deficits with perimetry.
objectives: Compare seizure freedom after at least 24 months of follow-up, postoperative complications, perimetry-confirmed visual field deficits, and cognitive outcomes after MRgLITT versus TLR.
Compare overall complications and complications categorized as minor when they resolve within 6 months or major when they persist beyond 6 months.

Assess whether the proportion of patients with mesial temporal lobe sclerosis (MTLS) is associated with overall seizure freedom and compare seizure freedom after the interventions among patients with MTLS.
In a post-hoc analysis, examine whether the MTLS proportion accounts for heterogeneity in seizure outcomes among TLR studies.
clinical_question: Patients: people with drug-resistant mTLE. Intervention: MRgLITT. Comparator: TLR, comprising anterior temporal lobectomy (ATL) and selective amygdalohippocampectomy (sAHE). Outcomes: seizure freedom, postoperative complications, perimetry-confirmed visual field deficits, and cognitive outcomes.
study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of original prospective and retrospective cohort studies. The authors pooled outcomes separately for MRgLITT and TLR rather than relying on direct comparisons between the procedures. The review followed the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews as CRD42023400355. PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane library were searched on February 27th, 2023.

population.description: Patients with drug-resistant mTLE treated with MRgLITT, ATL, or sAHE. The reported overall cohorts comprised 4606 TLR patients and 534 MRgLITT patients; outcome-specific cohorts differed.
inclusion_criteria: Peer-reviewed prospective or retrospective cohort studies published in English that evaluated MRgLITT, ATL, or sAHE in patients with drug-resistant mTLE.

Studies reporting at least one eligible outcome: seizure status assessed with Engel or International League Against Epilepsy scales after at least 24 months; VFDs assessed by perimetry; complications classified as transient or permanent, or described sufficiently to determine duration; or cognitive outcomes assessed using WMS-III LM-I or LM-II, California verbal learning test/Rey- auditory verbal learning test, or Boston Naming Test.
Studies including no fewer than 10 patients.
exclusion_criteria: Noncohort publications, including randomized controlled trials, controlled trials, predictive studies, and conference abstracts.
Studies focused on diagnoses other than drug-resistant mTLE.
Studies restricted to specific patient subgroups, such as patients with mesial temporal lobe sclerosis.
Repeated publications from the same patient cohort assessing the same outcome.

primary: Postoperative seizure freedom, defined as Engel I or International League Against Epilepsy 1 + 2 status.

Overall complication frequency and the frequencies of major complications persisting beyond 6 months and minor complications resolving within 6 months. Minor VFDs, affective disorders, and memory deficits were treated as expected adverse effects rather than complications.
Postoperative VFDs identified by perimetry and designated as such in the original studies, without an additional threshold for extent or severity.

Cognitive outcomes: contextual verbal memory assessed by WMS-III LM-I or LM-II; verbal learning and memory assessed by California verbal learning test/Rey- auditory verbal learning test; and confrontation naming assessed by Boston Naming Test.
secondary: Association between the MTLS ratio and overall seizure freedom.
Comparison of seizure freedom after MRgLITT versus TLR among patients with MTLS.

statistical_methods: Study proportions were synthesized separately for MRgLITT and TLR using inverse-variance effect sizes and random-effects models. A Z-test compared the pooled outcomes between procedures; reported P values were two-tailed, with values less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. Between-study heterogeneity was assessed using tau (s), I2, and a heterogeneity test; values over 50% were considered substantial. Baujat plots and leave-one-study-out influence analyses examined heterogeneity and sensitivity. Funnel plots and Egger’s regression test assessed potential publication bias; for complications, publication bias was assessed only for the overall rate. A subgroup analysis examined MTLS ratio and seizure freedom, and a post-hoc mixed-effects meta-regression used MTLS ratio and intervention type as moderators. Because individual patient data were unavailable, the MTLS ratio analysis assumed that patients followed for more than 24 months had the same MTLS rate as those without that follow-up. Cognitive outcomes were analyzed descriptively because testing methods and reported data differed across studies.
follow_up: At least 24 months for seizure outcomes; cognitive outcomes were eligible regardless of follow-up duration.
quality_assessment_tool: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for study quality and Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) for certainty of evidence and strength of recommendations.
interpretation: TLR achieved greater seizure freedom than MRgLITT at follow-up beyond 24 months, but it also had a significantly higher frequency of transient complications. Overall and major complication rates did not differ significantly. Visual field deficits showed a nonsignificant trend toward greater frequency after TLR; the limited MRgLITT data prevent a firm comparison. Confrontation naming appeared better preserved after MRgLITT, whereas variation among studies precludes a firm conclusion about verbal learning and memory. The MTLS ratio was not significantly associated with seizure freedom and did not account for the heterogeneity in TLR seizure outcomes.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The seizure-freedom advantage for TLR agrees with an earlier meta-analysis that used shorter follow-up. The absence of a significant difference in overall and major complications is also consistent with a previous meta-analysis. Cognitive findings resemble those of Kohlhase et al.: declines in verbal learning or memory occurred after procedures involving the dominant temporal lobe, while confrontation naming appeared more favorable after MRgLITT. A separate comparative study found better preservation of verbal memory after MRgLITT than after open resection, but the authors state that this finding needs replication. Prior meta-analyses disagree about ATL versus sAHE: Hu et al. reported greater odds of seizure freedom with ATL, whereas Kuang et al., Xu et al., and Kohlhase et al. found no significant difference.
clinical_implications: The greater long-term seizure-freedom rate with TLR must be considered alongside its higher rate of minor or transient complications; the analysis did not find a higher rate of major complications than with MRgLITT.

The complications observed with TLR and MRgLITT differ in type. The authors suggest that those associated with TLR could be more severe, while acknowledging that they lack data on their effects on patients’ lives.
The possible visual-function advantage of MRgLITT remains uncertain because the difference in deficits was not statistically significant and perimetry data for MRgLITT were limited.
MRgLITT appears more favorable for confrontation naming. Whether it better preserves verbal memory remains uncertain.
The effectiveness of MRgLITT depends particularly on the epileptogenic zone being confined to the medial temporal lobe; TLR may be more suitable when that zone extends beyond it.
Transient complications after MRgLITT may permit faster recovery, although the authors present this as a possibility rather than an established outcome.
practice_implications: When long-term seizure freedom is the priority, TLR should be preferred over MRgLITT.
When preserving visual function is a particular concern, MRgLITT might be preferred, but the suggested advantage requires validation.
Interpret the relative merits of MRgLITT and TLR in light of each patient’s medical circumstances and in collaboration with the treating team.

Consider age and overall health when selecting an intervention: younger patients might tolerate open surgery better, whereas older patients might benefit from the lower frequency of minor complications with MRgLITT.
Interpret complication rates cautiously, particularly minor-complication rates, because reporting may be inconsistent or incomplete.
limitations: Only 2 MRgLITT studies contributed visual-field data, and the small number of patients assessed by perimetry limited statistical power and the conclusions possible for that outcome.
Substantial heterogeneity across several TLR outcomes limits generalizability. The MTLS-ratio analysis did not explain the heterogeneity in seizure outcomes.
Grouping ATL and sAHE as TLR increased the scope of the comparison but may conceal differences between the procedures.
Variation in neuropsychological methods, reported data, and criteria for significance restricted cognitive-outcome assessment to a descriptive comparison.
Differences in patient characteristics may have influenced which intervention was selected.
Restricting seizure analyses to longer follow-up may favor better outcomes if patients with worse outcomes were more likely to be lost, although most included studies had little loss to follow-up.

The MTLS subgroup analysis assumed that patients with more than 24 months of follow-up had the same MTLS ratio as those without that length of follow-up; the absence of individual patient data means this assumption could bias the findings.
TLR studies showed evidence of publication bias for seizure outcomes and visual field deficits. Limited MRgLITT visual-field data prevented a thorough bias assessment for that outcome.
Inconsistent complication definitions or reporting, particularly for transient events, may mean the reported rates do not capture their true frequency.

Combining studies with differing surgical techniques and patient characteristics may have contributed to heterogeneity. The absence of observed heterogeneity for major MRgLITT complications might also reflect an insufficiently comprehensive dataset.
strengths: Examining seizure outcomes at follow-up beyond 24 months addresses the shorter follow-up emphasized in previous analyses.
The analysis distinguished unexpected complications by duration from anticipated adverse effects and assessed visual field deficits identified by perimetry.
Sensitivity and influence analyses generally indicated that the findings for both interventions were not overly dependent on any single study.
open_questions: Whether MRgLITT genuinely results in fewer visual field deficits than TLR remains unresolved.
The relative effects of the interventions on verbal learning and memory require firmer evidence.
The source of the substantial heterogeneity in TLR outcomes remains unexplained.
The effects of the different complication types on patients’ lives are not established.
Whether ATL and sAHE have materially different outcomes within the pooled TLR category remains uncertain.
The relationship between MTLS and seizure outcomes needs assessment without the follow-up assumption used in this analysis.
future_directions: Conduct comparative TLR and MRgLITT studies that assess visual field deficits with formal perimetry, grade their extent, and record patient-relevant outcomes such as symptoms and effects on driving.
Use standardized cognitive-testing methods and comparative groups to permit more reliable assessment of temporal-lobe functions, including verbal memory and confrontation naming.
Study MTLS and seizure outcomes using individual patient data.
Improve the consistency of outcome and complication reporting across studies.
Replicate the comparative finding of better verbal-memory preservation after MRgLITT than after open resection.
Refine MRgLITT and other minimally invasive procedures, including radiofrequency thermocoagulation, to improve efficacy and safety.

main_findings.description: At 24 months after surgery, TLR had a higher pooled seizure-freedom proportion than MRgLITT.
main_findings.context: The analysis included 19 TLR studies and 6 MRgLITT studies. The observed proportions were 67.9% for TLR and 57.3% for MRgLITT. I2 was 90% for TLR and 11% for MRgLITT; the reported s2 values were 0.44 and <0.1, respectively. GRADE certainty was Very low for TLR and Low for MRgLITT.

main_findings.description: Perimetry-detected postoperative VFDs were numerically more frequent after TLR, but the between-intervention difference was not statistically significant.
main_findings.context: The analysis included 8 TLR studies and 2 MRgLITT studies. I2 was 88% for TLR and 65% for MRgLITT; the reported s2 values were 1.62 and 0.47, respectively. GRADE certainty was Very low for both interventions.

main_findings.description: The pooled overall complication rates did not differ significantly between TLR and MRgLITT.
main_findings.context: The analysis included 9 TLR studies and 5 MRgLITT studies. The observed complication proportions were 14.6% and 5.3%, respectively. I2 was 87% for TLR and 49% for MRgLITT; the reported s2 values were 0.40 and 0.31. GRADE certainty was Very low for both interventions. The supplementary GRADE assessment instead lists 205/1311 (15.6%) for TLR and 27/378 (7.1%) for MRgLITT.

main_findings.description: The pooled rates of major complications were not significantly different between interventions.
main_findings.context: The observed proportion was 2.1% in each group. I2 was 35% for TLR and 0% for MRgLITT; the reported s2 values were 0.35 and 0. GRADE certainty was Low for both interventions. The supplementary GRADE assessment instead lists 29/1311 (2.2%) for TLR and 15/378 (4.0%) for MRgLITT.

main_findings.description: TLR had a significantly higher pooled rate of minor complications than MRgLITT.
main_findings.context: The observed proportions were 12.4% for TLR and 3.2% for MRgLITT. I2 was 83% for TLR and 32% for MRgLITT; the reported s2 values were 0.38 and 0.29. GRADE certainty was Very low for both interventions. The supplementary GRADE assessment instead lists 176/1311 (13.4%) for TLR.

main_findings.description: After MRgLITT, the studies gave mixed findings for hippocampal-dependent cognition. Some reported significant group-level declines in verbal learning and delayed verbal memory, particularly after ablation of the dominant temporal lobe, while contextual memory was better preserved.
main_findings.value: 4 out of 6 studies reported declines in verbal learning/memory
main_findings.context: One study reported a significant decline in short delayed recall, particularly among patients with MTLS and larger ablated volumes in the dominant temporal lobe. Other studies found no significant group-level change but did observe individual declines; some improvements followed ablation in the non-dominant hemisphere. Two studies supplied no statistical-change data.

main_findings.description: Following MRgLITT, the reviewed studies did not report a decline in confrontation naming.
main_findings.context: The authors considered confrontation-naming outcomes more favorable with MRgLITT than with TLR.

main_findings.description: Following TLR in the dominant hemisphere, most studies reported a decline in verbal learning or memory.
main_findings.metric: Proportion of reviewed studies reporting decline
main_findings.context: Dominant-side TLR was most often left-sided. Non-dominant TLR, most often right-sided, could be followed by significant improvement in these functions. Two studies found no significant change in verbal learning or memory after TLR.

main_findings.description: Studies of confrontation naming after TLR differed: some reported a significant decline, whereas others found no significant change.
main_findings.metric: Proportion of reviewed studies reporting significant decline
main_findings.context: Differences in neuropsychological methods and reported data prevented a quantitative comparison of cognitive outcomes; the authors could not draw firm conclusions about verbal learning and memory.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Postoperative complications, random-effects pooled proportion: TLR 11.4% [7.4%, 17.2%] and MRgLITT 6.5% [3.3%, 12.3%]; between-intervention P value 0.15, not statistically significant. The observed counts were TLR 191/1311 (14.6%) and MRgLITT 20/378 (5.3%). Expected adverse effects were distinguished from complications.
notable_adverse_events: TLR major complications: 28/1311 (2.1%) observed; random-effects pooled proportion 2.0% [1.1%, 3.09%]. Hemiparesis accounted for 44% of major complications, and hydrocephalus requiring a shunt accounted for 33%. The authors state that some TLR major complications lacked enough detail to classify by type.
MRgLITT major complications: 8/378 (2.1%) observed; random-effects pooled proportion 2.7% [1.4%, 5.2%]. Diplopia accounted for 38% of major complications.

TLR minor complications: 163/1311 (12.4%) observed; random-effects pooled proportion 9.9% [6.4%, 15.0%]. Hematoma/hemorrhage accounted for 24% of minor complications, aphasia/dysphasia for 23%, and hemiparesis for 9%.
MRgLITT minor complications: 12/378 (3.2%) observed; random-effects pooled proportion 4.1% [1.9%, 8.4%]. Homonymous hemianopia accounted for 25% of minor complications and diplopia for 17%.

Perimetry-detected VFDs: TLR 345/490 patients, with a random-effects pooled proportion of 79.4% [59.5%, 91.0%]; MRgLITT 20/44 patients, with a pooled proportion of 49.8% [23.6%, 76.0%]. The difference was not statistically significant (P value 0.08). Minor VFDs were treated as expected adverse effects rather than complications.

subgroup_analyses: The MTLS analysis included 24 studies: 18 of TLR and 6 of MRgLITT. The MTLS ratio was not significantly associated with seizure freedom (P = 0.31).
Among patients with MTLS, seizure outcomes did not differ significantly between TLR and MRgLITT (P = 0.63).

In the TLR seizure-outcome analysis, the MTLS ratio was not a significant moderator of heterogeneity (P = 0.42); residual I2 was 94%. The observed between-study variability therefore remained unexplained by MTLS ratio.
secondary_results: The study-selection process yielded 55 included studies: MRgLITT = 14, ATL = 17, sAHE = 7, and ATL + sAHE = 17.

For the overall cohorts, Table 3 reports 4606 TLR patients and 534 MRgLITT patients. Mean age was 31 years for TLR and 42 years for MRgLITT; left-sided surgery was 48% and 55%; females comprised 52% and 54%; and MTLS was present in 59% and 71%, respectively. The reported Z-test P value for each of these four overall-cohort characteristic comparisons was <0.01.

Most included studies received high Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessments. The authors noted occasional shortcomings in complication and cognition outcome assessment and in accounting for loss to follow-up.

For seizure freedom, the funnel-plot regression test indicated publication bias in TLR (P < 0.01), but not significant evidence of publication bias in MRgLITT (P = 0.42). Omitting one study at a time gave TLR seizure-freedom proportions of 0.70 to 0.74, s2 of 0.30 to 0.48, and I2 of 87% to 91%; the corresponding MRgLITT ranges were 56% to 59%, 0.00 to 0.03, and 0% to 28%. The Baujat assessment identified Giovagnoli et al., 2016 as potentially influential for TLR heterogeneity and seizure-freedom effect.

For VFDs, the funnel-plot regression test indicated publication bias in TLR (P < 0.01). TLR leave-one-out analyses yielded VFD proportions of 74% to 83%, s2 of 1.09 to 2.08, and I2 of 86% to 89%. The authors identified Yam et al. as potentially influential for TLR VFD heterogeneity and proportion. With only 2 MRgLITT studies, the stated influence analysis and heterogeneity assessment were not applicable.

For overall complications, funnel-plot regression tests found no significant evidence of publication bias in TLR (P = 0.09) or MRgLITT (P = 0.87). TLR leave-one-out pooled overall complication proportions ranged from 10% to 13%, s2 from 0.28 to 0.45, and I2 from 68% to 89%. For MRgLITT, the paragraph describes the leave-one-out outcome as a major complication rate of 4.4% to 8.2%, with s2 of 0.00 to 0.45 and I2 of 0% to 62%, although it appears under overall complications. The authors identified Dorfer et al., 2017, Whiting et al., 2020, and Schmeiser et al., 2017 for TLR, and Le et al., 2018 for MRgLITT, as potentially influential for overall-complication heterogeneity and proportion.

For major complications, TLR leave-one-out pooled proportions ranged from 1.6% to 2.5%, s2 from 0.20 to 0.48, and I2 from 11% to 43%. The MRgLITT ranges were 2.1% to 3.0% for the pooled proportion and 0.00 to 0.06 for s2, with no change in I2.

For minor complications, TLR leave-one-out pooled proportions ranged from 8.7% to 11.1%, s2 from 0.28 to 0.35, and I2 from 65% to 85%. The MRgLITT ranges were 3.0% to 4.2%, 0.00 to 0.47, and 0% to 49%, respectively.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that both TLR and MRgLITT are effective and safe options for mTLE, but TLR achieves better long-term seizure freedom and has more minor complications. Overall and major complication rates are comparable; MRgLITT appears more favorable for confrontation naming, whereas the evidence does not permit a firm conclusion about verbal memory.
narrative_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared MRgLITT with TLR, grouping ATL and sAHE as resective surgery, in cohorts of patients with drug-resistant mTLE. The investigators examined seizure freedom after at least 24 months, perimetry-confirmed visual field deficits, complications classified by persistence, and cognitive outcomes. Random-effects estimates showed seizure freedom of 72.5% [65.6%, 78.5%] after TLR versus 57.1% [51.2%, 62.7%] after MRgLITT (P value <0.01). Visual field deficits were estimated at 79.4% [59.5%, 91.0%] and 49.8% [23.6%, 76.0%], respectively, but the difference was not statistically significant (P value: 0.08). Overall complication rates were 11.4% [7.4%, 17.2%] for TLR and 6.5% [3.3%, 12.3%] for MRgLITT (P value 0.15); major complication rates also did not differ significantly. Minor complications were more frequent after TLR: 9.9% [6.4%, 15.0%] versus 4.1% [1.9%, 8.4%] (P value 0.04). The authors consider TLR preferable when long-term seizure freedom is the priority, while MRgLITT may be considered when preserving visual function is especially important, pending confirmation of the nonsignificant visual-field trend. MRgLITT appears more favorable for confrontation naming, but heterogeneous cognitive evidence prevents firm conclusions about verbal memory. Limited MRgLITT perimetry data, substantial TLR heterogeneity, and potential selection and publication biases warrant caution when applying these findings to individual treatment decisions.

document_sections.heading: Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy versus Open Surgery for Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
document_sections.content: This review compares TLR with MRgLITT for drug-resistant mTLE, emphasizing seizure outcomes after more than 24 months, perimetry-confirmed visual field deficits, complications classified by duration, and cognition. Postoperative seizure freedom favored TLR: 72.5% [65.6%, 78.5%] versus 57.1% [51.2%, 62.7%] with MRgLITT (P value <0.01). Visual field deficits occurred in 79.4% [59.5%, 91.0%] after TLR and 49.8% [23.6%, 76.0%] after MRgLITT; this difference was not statistically significant (P value: 0.08). Overall complication estimates were 11.4% [7.4%, 17.2%] and 6.5% [3.3%, 12.3%], respectively (P value 0.15). Major complication estimates were 2.0% [1.1%, 3.09%] and 2.7% [1.4%, 5.2%] (P value 0.54). Minor complications were more frequent after TLR, at 9.9% [6.4%, 15.0%], than after MRgLITT, at 4.1% [1.9%, 8.4%] (P value 0.04). MRgLITT appeared more favorable for confrontation naming; evidence on verbal memory did not support a firm conclusion. The authors conclude that TLR provides better seizure control but more transient complications. They regard the visual field finding as a nonsignificant trend toward more deficits after TLR and describe their sensitivity analyses as supporting the stability of the findings.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Epilepsy affects up to 0.6% of the global population. Temporal lobe epilepsy often accompanies verbal and memory difficulties that further diminish quality of life. The authors describe mTLE as the most common form of DRE; seizures may remain frequent despite optimal antiseizure medication. Earlier evidence establishes TLR as more effective than medical management for drug-resistant mTLE, while MRgLITT offers a newer alternative. Few studies compare the procedures directly, motivating a meta-analysis of observational evidence. Penfield and Flanigan reported a temporal lobectomy series in 1950. Contemporary ATL generally limits lateral resection, preserves the superior temporal gyrus, and maximizes medial resection. Niemeyer introduced transcortical sAHE, and Yasargil subsequently introduced transsylvian sAHE. MRgLITT was first used for DRE in 2014. It involves inserting a 980 nm diode laser through a 3.2 mm burr hole to produce thermal injury, monitored with near-real-time magnetic resonance thermography and temperature markers intended to protect other tissue. This analysis groups ATL and sAHE as TLR. The interventions have differing efficacy and adverse-effect profiles, but direct comparisons are scarce. A prior meta-analysis by Kohlhase et al. suggested better Engel-I outcomes with ATL than MRgLITT and higher, nonsignificant overall and major complication rates with ATL. Other studies suggest better preservation of naming with MRgLITT, whereas evidence on verbal learning and memory is inadequate for definitive conclusions. Previous analyses often used shorter seizure follow-up. The authors identify longer follow-up, separation of complications from expected adverse effects, and careful visual field assessment as important for comparison.

document_sections.heading: MATERIALS AND METHODS
document_sections.content: The review followed the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis guidelines statement. Its PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews registration is CRD42023400355.

document_sections.heading: Search Strategy
document_sections.content: A PICOS framework defined the question: among people with drug-resistant mTLE, how do MRgLITT and TLR compare for seizure freedom, postoperative complications, visual field deficits, and cognition? Only original research was eligible. F.E. searched PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane library on February 27th, 2023. Supplement A provides the search terms.

document_sections.heading: Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
document_sections.content: Eligibility rules specified study design, diagnosis, interventions, reported outcomes, sample size, publication characteristics, and duplicate cohorts.

document_sections.heading: Inclusion Criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible publications were English-language, peer-reviewed prospective or retrospective cohort studies of MRgLITT, ATL, or sAHE for drug-resistant mTLE. They needed to report at least one specified outcome and include no fewer than 10 patients. Seizure outcomes required Engel or International League Against Epilepsy assessment and at least 24 months of follow-up. Visual field deficits required perimetry. Complications needed transient-versus-permanent classification or duration sufficient to distinguish minor events resolving within 6 months from major events persisting beyond 6 months. Cognitive outcomes could be reported at any follow-up time and included verbal memory measured with WMS-III LM-I or LM-II, verbal learning and memory measured with California verbal learning test/Rey- auditory verbal learning test, or confrontation naming measured with Boston Naming Test.

document_sections.heading: Exclusion Criteria
document_sections.content: The review excluded noncohort designs, including randomized controlled trials, controlled trials, predictive studies, and conference abstracts. It also excluded studies of diagnoses other than drug-resistant mTLE, studies restricted to particular subgroups such as patients with mesial temporal lobe sclerosis, repeated publications evaluating the same outcome in the same cohort, and publications before 2000.

document_sections.heading: Justifications
document_sections.content: The authors chose 24 months for seizure follow-up to capture longer-term outcomes while retaining enough studies. The minimum of 10 patients was intended to retain cohorts large enough to affect the synthesis. Randomized controlled trials, controlled trials, and predictive studies were excluded because their design and patient selection differed from cohort studies, complicating pooling and interpretation. The 2000 publication cutoff was intended to keep evidence relevant to contemporary practice.

document_sections.heading: Selection of Studies and Data Extraction
document_sections.content: The review describes title, abstract, and full-text selection followed by extraction of study characteristics, intervention types, and relevant outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection.
document_sections.content: The first author screened titles and abstracts, then assessed full texts not definitively excluded. Uncertain eligibility decisions were discussed with the senior author, D.N. The selection diagram reports Pubmed n=2076, Embase n=3353, and Cochrane n=73 records; n = 1441 duplicates were removed. It reports n =4061 records screened, n = 3818 excluded by title or abstract, n = 243 reports sought, n = 4 unavailable, and n = 239 assessed for eligibility. Full-text exclusions were out of scope (n = 12), the same cohort (n = 5), or other inclusion/exclusion criteria (n = 167). The diagram reports n = 55 included studies: MRgLITT = 14, ATL = 17, sAHE = 7, and ATL + sAHE = 17.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction.
document_sections.content: The extracted information comprised authorship, publication year, study sample and participant characteristics, intervention type, seizure outcomes, complications, visual field deficits, and cognition. Data were managed in Microsoft Excel.

document_sections.heading: Endpoints
document_sections.content: Primary outcomes were seizure freedom, complications, perimetry-identified visual field deficits, and specified cognitive test outcomes. Seizure freedom meant Engel I or International League Against Epilepsy 1 + 2. Complications were unwanted, unexpected, uncommon postoperative events. Adapting the Rydenhag and Silander classification in line with Bjellvi et al., the authors extended its duration boundary from 3 months to 6 months: major complications persisted for more than 6 months or were called persistent in source studies; minor complications resolved within 6 months or were called transient. Minor visual field deficits, affective disorders, and memory deficits were treated as expected adverse effects rather than complications. Visual field deficits were those explicitly identified by source studies; no further threshold for extent or severity was imposed. Cognitive measures were WMS-III LM-I or LM-II for contextual verbal memory, California verbal learning test/Rey- auditory verbal learning test for verbal learning and memory, and Boston Naming Test for confrontation naming. Secondary endpoints examined whether the MTLS ratio related to overall seizure freedom and compared seizure freedom between procedures among patients with MTLS.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Analyses used R (version 4.3.1), the meta package (6.5e 0), the metafor package (4.2e0), and the forestplot package (3.1.1). Study proportions and inverse-variance effect sizes were synthesized separately for MRgLITT and TLR with random-effects models. A Z-test compared outcomes between interventions. Tau (s) and I2 assessed heterogeneity; values over 50% indicated substantial heterogeneity. The authors also tested heterogeneity, used Baujat plots to identify influential contributors, and assessed how excluding each study affected pooled effects and heterogeneity. Funnel plot inspection and Egger’s regression test assessed possible publication bias. Reported P values were two-tailed; values less than 0.05 were considered significant. Publication-bias assessment for complications covered only overall complications because source studies did not uniformly distinguish major from minor events.

document_sections.heading: Subgroup Analysis
document_sections.content: The authors examined whether the MTLS ratio related to seizure freedom or modified the apparent effectiveness of MRgLITT and TLR. Because seizure outcomes after TLR were highly heterogeneous, a post-hoc mixed-effects meta-regression included MTLS ratio and intervention type as moderators. MTLS ratio came from each whole cohort. With individual patient data unavailable, the analysis assumed that patients followed for more than 24 months had the same MTLS rate as patients without that length of follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Quality Assessment
document_sections.content: The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale evaluated participant selection, group comparability, and outcome ascertainment, with more stars representing higher study quality. The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) approach assessed evidence certainty and recommendation strength by considering study limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and reporting bias.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS Literature Search and Descriptive Analysis
document_sections.content: The selection process yielded 55 studies. The study-characteristics table presents overall and outcome-specific TLR and MRgLITT cohorts and compares their reported characteristics.

document_sections.heading: GRADE Assessment and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. GRADE: Summary of Findings
document_sections.content: Table 1 presents observational-study counts, outcome proportions, and GRADE certainty separately for TLR and MRgLITT across seizure freedom, visual field deficits, and overall, major, and minor complications. Its complication counts differ from those in the supplementary GRADE assessment.

document_sections.heading: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
document_sections.content: Most included studies received high Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessments. The authors noted occasional deficiencies in assessing complications and cognition and in accounting for loss to follow-up. Supplement C is cited for study-level detail.

document_sections.heading: Meta-Analysis Summary Table
document_sections.content: Table 2 summarizes random-effects outcome proportions and confidence intervals for each intervention, between-intervention P values, and heterogeneity estimates for seizure freedom, visual field deficits, and overall, major, and minor complications.

document_sections.heading: Detailed Results for Individual Outcomes.
document_sections.content: The authors refer readers to Supplement C for individual-study data and forest plots underlying the outcome analyses.

document_sections.heading: Seizure Outcome.
document_sections.content: The TLR analysis included 19 studies and 3031 patients; 2057 reached Engel I at 24 months after surgery. TLR study heterogeneity was high (I2 90%). The MRgLITT analysis included 6 studies and 288 patients; 165 reached Engel I at 24 months, with low heterogeneity (I2 11%). The between-intervention Z-test gave P value <0.01, favoring TLR for seizure freedom at 24 months. Table 3 describes the cohorts contributing to the outcome analyses.

document_sections.heading: Visual Field Deficits.
document_sections.content: For TLR, 8 studies included 490 patients, of whom 345 had a postoperative deficit confirmed by perimetry; heterogeneity was high (I2 88%). For MRgLITT, 2 studies included 44 patients, of whom 20 developed a postoperative deficit; heterogeneity was moderate-high (I2 65%). The comparison yielded P-value 0.08 and was not significant at a = 0.05.

document_sections.heading: Complications Outcome.
document_sections.content: Complication analyses drew on 9 TLR studies with 1311 patients and 5 MRgLITT studies with 378 patients. Outcomes were separated into overall, major, and minor complications.

document_sections.heading: Overall Complications.
document_sections.content: The main results report 191 complications (14.6%) after TLR and 20 (5.3%) after MRgLITT. The Z-test gave P value (0.15), without a significant between-intervention difference. Heterogeneity was high for TLR (I2 87%) and moderate for MRgLITT (I2 49%). Supplement A reports different overall complication counts; the document does not reconcile them.

document_sections.heading: Major Complications.
document_sections.content: The main results record 28 major complications (2.1%) after TLR. Hemiparesis accounted for 44% of those complications, and hydrocephalus requiring a shunt for 33%. MRgLITT had 8 major complications (2.1%), most commonly diplopia (38%). The between-group P value was 0.54, without a significant difference. Heterogeneity was I2 35% for TLR and I2 0% for MRgLITT. Some TLR major complications could not be assigned a type because source studies lacked descriptions. Supplement A gives different major-complication counts from the main results.

document_sections.heading: Minor Complications.
document_sections.content: The main results record 163 minor complications (12.4%) after TLR. The most common were hematoma/hemorrhage (24% of complications), aphasia/dysphasia (23%), and hemiparesis (9%). After MRgLITT, 12 minor complications (3.2%) were recorded, most commonly homonymous hemianopia (25%) and diplopia (17%). TLR had a significantly higher minor-complication rate (P-value 0.04). Heterogeneity was I2 83% for TLR and I2 32% for MRgLITT. Supplement A reports a different TLR minor-complication count.

document_sections.heading: Neuropsychological Outcomes
document_sections.content: Differences in neuropsychological methods and reported data prevented quantitative synthesis, so cognition was described narratively. Following MRgLITT, studies reported mixed outcomes in hippocampal-dependent functions. Some reported significant group-level declines in verbal learning and delayed verbal memory, particularly after dominant temporal lobe ablation, while contextual memory was better preserved. One study found significantly worse short delayed recall, especially with MTLS and larger dominant-sided ablation volumes. Other studies reported no significant group-level changes despite individual declines; some improvements followed nondominant ablation. Two studies supplied no statistical-change data. Overall, four out of six MRgLITT studies observed verbal learning or memory decline, and none observed confrontation-naming decline. After TLR, dominant-sided resection often reduced verbal memory, while nondominant resection could significantly improve it. Two studies found no significant verbal learning or memory change. Confrontation naming declined in some TLR studies but did not change significantly in others. Overall, 7 of 9 studies reported verbal learning or memory decline after dominant-hemisphere resection, and 2 out of 4 found significant confrontation-naming decline.

document_sections.heading: MTLS Subgroup Analyses
document_sections.content: The MTLS analysis included 24 studies: 18 TLR and 6 MRgLITT. MTLS ratio was not significantly associated with seizure freedom (P = 0.31), and seizure outcome did not differ significantly between interventions in the MTLS group (P = 0.63). The model for TLR seizure outcomes retained substantial heterogeneity (I2 94%). MTLS ratio was not a significant moderator of that heterogeneity (P = 0.42), leaving its source unexplained.

document_sections.heading: Sensitivity Analysis Summary
document_sections.content: The authors refer to Supplement D for plots associated with the sensitivity analyses.

document_sections.heading: Seizure Outcome.
document_sections.content: The funnel-asymmetry regression indicated publication bias for TLR seizure outcomes (P < 0.01), but not for MRgLITT (P = 0.42). Leaving out individual TLR studies produced seizure-freedom proportions of 0.70 to 0.74, s2 values of 0.30 to 0.48, and I2 values of 87% to 91%. Corresponding MRgLITT ranges were 56% to 59%, 0.00 to 0.03, and 0% to 28%. The TLR Baujat plot suggested that Giovagnoli et al., 2016 might influence both heterogeneity and the seizure-freedom estimate.

document_sections.heading: Visual Field Deficit.
document_sections.content: The TLR funnel-asymmetry regression suggested publication bias (P < 0.01). Leaving out individual TLR studies yielded visual field deficit proportions of 74% to 83%, s2 values of 1.09 to 2.08, and I2 values of 86% to 89%. The TLR Baujat plot identified Yam et al. as potentially influential for heterogeneity and the deficit estimate. With only 2 MRgLITT studies, the authors state that influence and heterogeneity assessment was not applicable.

document_sections.heading: Complication.
document_sections.content: Funnel-asymmetry testing did not find significant publication-bias evidence for TLR complications (P = 0.09) or MRgLITT complications (P = 0.87).

document_sections.heading: Overall Complications.
document_sections.content: Leaving out individual TLR studies yielded pooled overall-complication proportions of 10% to 13%, s2 values of 0.28 to 0.45, and I2 values of 68% to 89%. For MRgLITT, this paragraph describes an influence-analysis range of 4.4% to 8.2% as a major-complication rate, although it appears under overall complications; its s2 values were 0.00 to 0.45 and I2 values 0% to 62%. The Baujat plots suggested possible influence on overall-complication heterogeneity and estimates from Dorfer et al., 2017, Whiting et al., 2020, and Schmeiser et al., 2017 for TLR, and Le et al., 2018 for MRgLITT.

document_sections.heading: Major Complications.
document_sections.content: Leaving out individual studies produced TLR pooled major-complication proportions of 1.6% to 2.5%, s2 values of 0.20 to 0.48, and I2 values of 11% to 43%. MRgLITT estimates ranged from 2.1% to 3.0%, with s2 values of 0.00 to 0.06 and no change in I2.

document_sections.heading: Minor Complications.
document_sections.content: Leaving out individual studies produced TLR pooled minor-complication proportions of 8.7% to 11.1%, s2 values of 0.28 to 0.35, and I2 values of 65% to 85%. MRgLITT ranges were 3.0% to 4.2%, 0.00 to 0.47, and 0% to 49%, respectively.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: The authors interpret TLR as providing better seizure freedom beyond 24 months, consistent with a previously published meta-analysis using shorter follow-up. They consider postoperative visual field deficit rates comparable statistically, despite a nonsignificant trend favoring MRgLITT. The incidence after MRgLITT, reported by only 2 studies, was higher than they expected. They describe possible MRgLITT injury to the optic radiation through excessive ablation or catheter placement and possible injury to the optic tract or lateral geniculate nucleus through catheter misplacement, heat, or cytotoxic edema. Overall and major complication rates did not differ significantly, consistent with a prior meta-analysis, although TLR had numerically more overall events. TLR produced significantly more transient complications. MRgLITT appeared better for confrontation naming; heterogeneous studies precluded firm conclusions about verbal learning and memory. Among TLR major complications, hemiparesis and shunt-requiring hydrocephalus together accounted for 77%. The authors link these complications largely to structures at risk during resection, including the anterior choroidal artery and temporal-horn access. They associate MRgLITT complications with possible thermal injury to the oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve, or optic tract. Diplopia comprised 38% of MRgLITT major complications. Without data on patients’ lived impact, they suggest that TLR complications might be more severe but do not establish that comparison. Hemorrhage/hematoma, aphasia/dysphasia, and hemiparesis together represented 56% of TLR minor complications; homonymous hemianopia and diplopia represented 42% after MRgLITT. Their separation of expected adverse effects from unexpected complications was intended to isolate the latter, not to imply that expected effects discussed during presurgical counseling are unimportant. Their cognitive findings align with Kohlhase et al.: 4 out of 6 MRgLITT studies reported significant group-level verbal learning and/or delayed-recall decline, but none reported confrontation-naming decline; after dominant-sided TLR, 7 out of 9 studies found significant verbal-learning decline, and 2 out of 4 found significant naming decline. The authors call for standardized comparative studies. They cite one comparative study reporting better preservation of verbal memory after MRgLITT than open resection and say replication is needed. ATL and sAHE were combined to improve statistical power and external validity, potentially concealing procedure-specific differences. Hu et al. reported higher odds of seizure freedom with ATL than sAHE, whereas Kuang et al., Xu et al., and Kohlhase et al. reported no significant difference.

document_sections.heading: MTLS Subgroup Analysis
document_sections.content: The subgroup analysis found no significant relationship between MTLS and overall seizure freedom or between intervention and seizure freedom among patients with MTLS. Assuming the same MTLS ratio for patients with and without more than 24 months of follow-up could bias these findings. Individual-patient data might clarify the relationship.

document_sections.heading: Implications for Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: The authors state that TLR should be preferred when long-term seizure freedom is the priority. MRgLITT might be preferred when preserving visual function is particularly important, but its apparent visual field advantage is nonsignificant and requires validation. TLR carries more transient or minor complications without a higher observed major-complication rate; the authors suggest serious-complication risks may be similar and recovery after MRgLITT complications may be faster. They note indications, rather than a firm conclusion, that MRgLITT may better preserve verbal memory. Choice should reflect the individual patient's circumstances and discussion with the treating team. They state that MRgLITT effectiveness depends particularly on an epileptogenic zone confined to the medial temporal lobe; TLR may be more viable when it extends beyond that region. Age and general health also matter: younger patients might tolerate open surgery better, whereas older patients might benefit from MRgLITT's minor-complication profile.

document_sections.heading: Stability and Reliability of the Results
document_sections.content: Heterogeneity varied by outcome and intervention and was substantial for several TLR outcomes. Combining resection techniques might contribute, although another meta-analysis also found high heterogeneity when assessing ATL and sAHE separately. MTLS ratio did not explain heterogeneity in TLR seizure outcomes. MRgLITT generally had low-to-moderate heterogeneity; zero observed heterogeneity for its major complications could reflect stable results or an insufficient dataset. Different techniques, patient characteristics, and inconsistent complication definitions or reporting could explain variation, particularly for TLR. Transient minor events may be underreported, so reported complication rates—especially minor-event rates—require caution. Significant publication-bias evidence for TLR seizure and visual field outcomes also warrants caution; the authors note that favorable outcomes might be overrepresented. They found no comparable bias signal for MRgLITT seizure outcomes or complications, while too few visual field studies prevented thorough assessment. Influence analyses suggested that neither intervention's findings depended excessively on a single study, although TLR heterogeneity remains unexplained. The authors call particularly for comparative studies using formal perimetry. A large MRgLITT cohort published after the search reported seizure and complication findings similar to theirs; they judge its omission unlikely to materially alter their conclusions.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Few MRgLITT patients underwent perimetry, limiting power and interpretation of the visual field comparison. Larger cohorts are needed with formal perimetry, deficit grading, subjective symptoms, and driving-related outcomes. Substantial, unexplained TLR heterogeneity may limit generalizability and motivates more standardized reporting. Cognitive results could only be compared descriptively because reporting practices and criteria for statistical significance varied. Intervention selection according to individual characteristics might introduce bias. Restricting seizure analyses to longer-followed patients might favor better outcomes if those with poorer outcomes were more likely to be lost, although Newcastle-Ottawa Scale assessments indicated little loss to follow-up in most studies.

document_sections.heading: Future Directions in the Surgical Treatment of Temporal Lobe Epilepsy
document_sections.content: The authors describe advances toward more precise, minimally invasive surgery. Laser ablation is a viable option for temporal lobe epilepsy despite lower seizure-freedom rates. They call for improved techniques and more consistent visual field and cognitive data after laser treatment. A wider range of operations may make surgery acceptable to patients previously reluctant to undergo an open procedure.

document_sections.heading: In-Depth Analysis of VFD Rates:
document_sections.content: Further perimetry-based investigation of visual field deficits after MRgLITT is needed to clarify how its rates compare with TLR.

document_sections.heading: Standardized Cognitive Testing Protocols:
document_sections.content: The authors advocate standardized cognitive assessments in studies with comparative groups so that temporal-lobe-related cognitive outcomes can be compared more reliably.

document_sections.heading: Optimizing Minimally Invasive Techniques:
document_sections.content: Further research should refine MRgLITT and other relatively new minimally invasive approaches, including radiofrequency thermocoagulation, to improve efficacy and safety.

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: The authors regard both TLR and MRgLITT as effective and safe treatments for mTLE. TLR provides better long-term seizure freedom. Overall and major complication rates appear comparable, while minor complications are more frequent after TLR. MRgLITT appears more favorable for confrontation naming; verbal-memory effects need further study before firm conclusions are possible.

document_sections.heading: Supplement A. GRADE Assessment
document_sections.content: The supplementary assessment tabulates observational evidence, study counts, patient outcome proportions, and certainty separately for TLR and MRgLITT. It reports different complication counts and proportions from the main text and Table 1, without explaining the discrepancies. Its certainty assessments are Very low for TLR seizure freedom and Low for MRgLITT seizure freedom; visual field deficits and overall and minor complications are Very low for both interventions, while major complications are Low for both.

document_sections.heading: Explanations
document_sections.content: The supplementary GRADE explanations downgrade TLR seizure-freedom certainty for unexplained heterogeneity (I^2 = 90%) and significant publication bias. For visual field deficits, they cite TLR heterogeneity (I2 = 88%), a wide TLR 95% interval of 60% to 91%, and TLR publication bias. For TLR overall complications, they cite heterogeneity (I^2 = 84%) and a wide 95% interval of 8.1% to 18.1%. Further explanations cite a 95% interval of 6.7% to 16.0% for TLR minor complications and a heterogeneity value of I2 = 81% in the supplementary material's disordered sequence of TLR complication explanations; those statements are not unambiguously attached to the same outcome there. For MRgLITT visual field deficits, the explanations cite heterogeneity (I2 = 65%) and substantial imprecision because only 2 studies with 44 patients were included. For MRgLITT overall complications, they cite heterogeneity (I2 = 49%) and a 95% interval of 3.3% to 12.3%. For MRgLITT minor complications, they cite a 95% interval of 1.9% to 8.4% as serious imprecision. These explanations include heterogeneity figures that do not all agree with the main analysis.

document_sections.heading: Supplement B. Newcastle-Ottawa-scale
document_sections.content: The supplementary tables present study-by-study Newcastle-Ottawa-scale assessments of cohort selection, exposure and outcome ascertainment, follow-up, and applicable comparison criteria. The authors adapted scoring to this review: selection of an unexposed cohort did not apply to studies without a control group; within-study cohort-comparability analyses were not central to this synthesis, although characteristics were collected for context. Stars for outcome assessment were reserved for seizure and visual field outcomes, which the authors considered objective, and were not awarded for complications or cognition merely because a study also reported an objective outcome. Studies losing more than 20% of patients to follow-up received no adequacy-of-follow-up star.

document_sections.heading: Literature search and search terms
document_sections.content: The supplement supplies database-specific search expressions for temporal lobe epilepsy and MRgLITT or resective operations, together with terms excluding reviews, meta-analyses, conference abstracts, and case reports.

document_sections.heading: PUBMED
document_sections.content: The PubMed strategy combined the epilepsy population with laser treatment, ATL, or amygdalohippocampectomy terms, then applied publication-type exclusions. Its February 27th, 2023 search returned 2076 records.

document_sections.heading: EMBASE
document_sections.content: The Embase strategy combined temporal lobe epilepsy terms with laser and resection procedure terms and excluded specified nonoriginal publication types. Its February 27th, 2023 search returned 3353 records.

document_sections.heading: COCHRANE LIBRARY
document_sections.content: The Cochrane library strategy combined temporal lobe epilepsy with laser or resective intervention terms and excluded specified review, conference, and case-report terms. Its February 27th, 2023 search returned 73 records. The supplementary search summary gives 5502 records before duplicate removal, 4061 afterward, 243 after title-and-abstract screening, and 55 after full-text assessment.

document_sections.heading: SUPPLEMENT D Data on primary outcomes.
document_sections.content: This supplement identifies outcome displays for seizure freedom, overall, major, and minor complications, and visual field deficits, separately for TLR and MRgLITT. The provided content adds no outcome estimates beyond those reported elsewhere.

document_sections.heading: SUPPLEMENT E Sensitivity analyses.
document_sections.content: This supplement identifies funnel and Baujat plots for seizure outcomes in each intervention group, complications in each intervention group, and TLR visual field deficits. The provided content supplies no additional numerical sensitivity results.
